Project Overview: Gamified Literacy Ecosystem for Early Learners

As the Product Owner and Designer, I spearheaded the development of a pedagogical reading platform specifically engineered for the cognitive and motor-skill requirements of children aged 2 to 6. This project wasn't just about "reading books", it was about building a scalable educational framework that balances parental oversight with child-led exploration.

I synthesised longitudinal data from my previous "Spring-A-Story" project to identify a key market gap: most literacy apps are either too passive (videos) or too complex (cluttered UI). My goal was to create a "Goldilocks" experience: high engagement with zero cognitive overload.

1. Strategic Discovery & Product Roadmapping

I approached the "Brainstorming" phase from a Technical Product Manager perspective, defining the MVP (Minimum Viable Product) based on three core pillars: Phonetic Recognition, Engagement Loops, and Accessibility Standards.

  • Gamification Architecture: I designed a tiered progression system where levels are unlocked via "Mastery Points." This ensures the child is not overwhelmed by content beyond their current reading age.
  • Performance Analytics: For the parental dashboard, I specified the back-end requirements to track "Struggle Words"—specific phonemes where the child hesitates—allowing for personalised AI-driven reading recommendations.
  • Feature Prioritisation: Using a MoSCoW matrix, I prioritised "Voice-to-Text validation" and "Haptic Feedback" as P0 features to ensure an interactive learning loop.

2. Interaction Design (IxD) & UX Flow

Designing for a 2-year-old requires a radical departure from standard UI patterns. I focused on Affordance and Feedback:

  • Motor Skill Optimisation: I replaced small button targets with large "Touch Zones" and swipe gestures, acknowledging that fine motor control is still developing in this demographic.
  • Audio-Visual Synchronisation: I architected a "Follow-the-Bounce" highlight system. As the app narrates, the text scales and changes colour, reinforcing the connection between spoken word and written symbol.
  • The "Safety First" Flow: I designed a "Gated" navigation system for settings and external links to ensure children cannot accidentally exit the learning environment or make in-app purchases.

3. Iterative Prototyping: From Sketches to Low-Fi

In the wireframing phase, I experimented with Horizontal vs. Vertical storytelling. Through rapid paper prototyping, I discovered that horizontal layouts better mimicked the physical book experience, aiding in the mental transition from digital to physical literacy.

  • Component Library Development: I built a modular set of UI components (Navigation Orbs, Reward Badges, and Story Cards) to ensure design consistency and faster developer handoff.
  • Cognitive Load Reduction: I removed all non-essential UI during the actual reading flow. No battery indicators, no clocks, no menus—just the child and the story.

4. High-Fidelity Execution & Design System

The Adobe XD prototype serves as the "Source of Truth" for the final build. I transitioned into a UI Design focus here, employing high-contrast, child-safe colour palettes and accessible typography (using rounded, sans-serif fonts like Andika which are proven to aid dyslexic and early learners).

  • Visual Rewards System: I integrated "Micro-Animations" for every page completion. Using Lottie animations, we provide instant positive reinforcement through a visual "Star Explosion" and auditory cheers.
  • State Management: I designed the UI states for "Active Reading," "Error/Struggle," and "Success," ensuring the app intuitively guides the child back to the correct path without parental intervention.

5. Technical Retrospective & Scalability

As the Product Owner, my vision for this project extends beyond a static app. The high-fidelity prototype is currently undergoing "User Testing" with a small cohort of parents to validate the following KPIs:

  1. Time-to-Completion: Are children finishing stories without frustration?
  2. Word Retention: Is the "Struggle Word" logic effectively resurfacing difficult terms in subsequent sessions?
  3. App Stickiness: Does the gamified level system encourage daily usage?

Future Roadmap: To explore Speech Recognition API integration to allow the app to "listen" to the child and provide real-time phonetic correction—truly bridging the gap between a digital tool and a personal tutor.

childMarkdownRemark.html: To design a UI for a React Native reading book application for young children, based off the existing Spring-A-Story web application. The main purpose is to make the application more user-friendly for commercial use, while also enhancing the user experience.
